4.1. Sample description


The initial sample of equity o!erings is obtained from Securities Data Corporation, and consists of 2995 seasoned underwritten primary and secondary
o!erings between January 1983 and December 1992. I exclude "rms making

shelf o!erings and combination o!erings of equity and other securities. Further,
utilities and "nancial companies are excluded as, owing to greater regulation for
these "rms, their ability to engage in earnings management might di!er from
those of industrial "rms. For inclusion in the "nal sample, the issuing "rms must
have accounting data on the 1998 quarterly COMPUSTAT database.

For each equity o!ering in the sample, the "rst public announcement of the
o!ering is obtained by searching the Dow Jones Text and LEXIS online
services. To avoid confounding e!ects, issuers with another major news release
occurring between the day preceding and the day following the o!ering announcement day are excluded. The data for stock returns are from the University of Chicago's Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) daily "les.
Finally, as a matter of notation, I de"ne event quarter !1 as the "scal quarter
for which earnings were last announced before an equity o!ering announcement. All other quarters are identi"ed relative to this quarter.

Dechow et al. (1996) suggest that managers of "rms that require frequent
external "nancing will report earnings conservatively to create a positive reputation in the market, from which they can bene"t in subsequent o!erings. Since the
incentives of "rms frequently raising external capital may di!er from those of
other "rms, frequent issuers are excluded from the analyses. Frequent issuers are
de"ned as "rms with more than one public o!ering of seasoned common stock
in a two-year period. This de"nition is based on the belief that an o!ering made
within two years of another o!ering may be anticipated at the time of the earlier
o!ering, which may change a manager's incentives to engage in earnings
management. The sample of frequent o!erings consists of 437 o!erings by 191
"rms.�

Panel A of Table 1 presents the distribution of the non-frequent o!erings
across various years. There are 1222 equity o!erings in the sample. Four of the
sample years (1983, 1986, 1991 and 1992) are very active, and contain more than
10% of the sample. The highest level of equity issuance is in the hot issue market
of 1983, which accounts for nearly 24% of the sample. Panel B of this table
summarizes the issue and issuer characteristics. The mean and median equity
capitalization prior to the o!erings are $534.8 million and $121.4 million
respectively, indicating the presence of a few large "rms in the sample. For the
median "rm, an equity o!ering raises $27 million and results in a 20% increase
in the number of shares outstanding.

- Since frequent issuers are not known ex-ante, excluding these "rms from the analyses could
induce a forward-looking bias. Hence, I repeated the tests with the "rst o!ering by each frequent
issuer included in the sample of &non-frequent' o!erings. This inclusion has no signi"cant impact on
the qualitative results.
